summary:
We developed the Lunar Landing Site Navigator, an interactive web application designed to evaluate and compare potential landing sites across the Moon’s South Pole. By combining NASA lunar topography and ephemeris data with real-time 3D Sun, Earth, and Moon visualizations, the platform calculates solar elevation angles, direct-to-Earth communication windows, power generation based on lander solar array configurations, and optimal landing dates.
Existing tools like JPL Horizons and QuickMap require navigating complex interfaces and raw datasets, slowing down rapid scenario evaluation. Our tool streamlines this process into a single intuitive dashboard featuring an interactive timeline slider, side-by-side site comparison, and automated window recommendations.
At the lunar South Pole, steep terrain, extreme shadows, and shifting orbital geometry mean small changes in location or launch date can threaten mission survival. Our platform empowers mission planners, educators, and the public to quickly assess trade-offs and ensure safe, sustainable lunar operations.

Project Details :


What the Project Does

The Lunar Landing Site Navigator helps users explore possible landing sites near the Moon’s South Pole. Select a location on the 3D Moon to see information about its terrain, sunlight, communication with Earth, and power needs.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The website brings important mission information together in one place, making it easier to compare sites and spot potential risks. Our goal is to support safer, better-informed planning for future lunar missions.

Tools and Technologies

We built the website with React, JavaScript, and Three.js. The analysis and API use Python and FastAPI. The project uses NASA lunar terrain and sunlight data, JPL data about the Sun and Earth, and a machine-learning model to help estimate site suitability.

What Makes It Creative

Users can explore the Moon in 3D, click locations to view results, and adjust mission timing and lander hardware to see how those choices affect a site.

Factors We Considered

We considered terrain steepness and hazards, sunlight and darkness, communication with Earth, solar power and battery needs, safety margins, and uncertainty in the data. The tool supports early exploration and planning; it is not a certified landing decision system.
